cases.title: The Scrolls in the Cave
cases.summary: A shepherd hears something break inside a cave by the Dead Sea.
cases.brief: A young shepherd threw a stone into a cave and heard something made of clay break. Inside there were very old scrolls. Now we need to know what container they were kept in.
cases.objective: What container were the scrolls kept in?

evidence.title: The Qumran hills
evidence.description: Brown rocky hills by the Dead Sea, full of caves.

evidence.title: The young shepherd
evidence.description: A Bedouin shepherd was looking for a lost goat among the rocks.

evidence.title: The cave entrance
evidence.description: A small hole in the rock, barely big enough for a person.

evidence.title: Round pot
evidence.description: Reddish clay jug, short and round-bellied, with one curved handle. It is about 20 centimeters tall.

evidence.title: Woven basket
evidence.description: Round, wide basket woven from dry palm leaves. It is straw colored.

evidence.title: Tall jar
evidence.description: Pale clay jar about 60 centimeters tall, with a slightly chipped rim. On top it has a separate piece, also made of clay.

evidence.title: An open scroll
evidence.description: Leather scroll with columns of ancient letters. It is the book of Isaiah.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What the shepherd told about the cave.

doc.body: The shepherd Muhammad edh-Dhib was looking for a goat. He threw a stone into the cave and heard something made of clay break. Inside there were tall jars, and some of them were covered. The scrolls were inside!

evidence.title: Message from Tomás
evidence.description: Tomás saw a jar at the museum just like the ones in the cave.

doc.body: Professor: at the museum I saw a jar from the cave. It is tall and narrow, like a tube. On top it has a lid that looks like an upside-down bowl. That way the dust could not get in!

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the container from cave 1.

doc.body: It held leather scrolls, some of them wrapped in linen cloth.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: The world hears about the find.

doc.headline: Very old scrolls found by the Dead Sea
doc.body: Some shepherds found scrolls in a cave. One of them has the whole book of Isaiah and is much older than any copy known until now.

cases.wrongAccusation: Look again at Elena's notebook and Tomás's message: what was the container made of, how tall was it, and what did it have on top?

reward.title: The Dead Sea Scrolls
reward.copy: Between 1946 and 1947, a young Bedouin shepherd, Muhammad edh-Dhib, found clay jars with very old scrolls in a cave at Qumran. Later, many more scrolls turned up in other caves nearby. The most famous is the Great Isaiah Scroll: the whole book, copied by hand more than two thousand years ago, about seven meters long. Its text is almost the same as the one we read today. Isaiah 53 tells of the Servant who suffers for others. Today the scroll is kept at the Shrine of the Book, in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

cases.title: The Letters in the Tunnel
cases.summary: A boy finds letters carved into the wall of a tunnel full of water.
cases.brief: In 1880, a boy was walking through an ancient tunnel in Jerusalem, with water up to his knees. On the wall he saw letters carved into the rock. Now we need to know what story those letters tell.
cases.objective: What scene does the tunnel inscription tell?

evidence.title: The City of David
evidence.description: The oldest part of Jerusalem, on a hill.

evidence.title: Inside the tunnel
evidence.description: A narrow passage cut into the rock, with water running along the floor.

evidence.title: The inscription
evidence.description: Six lines of ancient Hebrew letters carved into a smooth stone.

evidence.title: Scene A
evidence.description: Drawing: a stonecutter with an iron pickaxe inside a dark tunnel. An oil lamp lights the rock.

evidence.title: Scene B
evidence.description: Drawing: workers in tunics stack big stones to build a wall, under the blue sky.

evidence.title: Scene C
evidence.description: Drawing: a rock hill seen from the inside. There are stonecutters with pickaxes and lamps at both ends of a tunnel, and a thin wall of rock is left between them.

evidence.title: Scene D
evidence.description: Drawing: women in long robes fill clay jars at a stone spring.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What the letters say, in simple words.

doc.body: Two groups of stonecutters dug with pickaxes, each toward the other. When they were almost there, they heard each other's voices through the rock. They met, and the water flowed from the spring to the pool.

evidence.title: Message from Lía
evidence.description: Lía and Tomás walked through the tunnel with flashlights.

doc.body: Professor: we walked the tunnel with flashlights. It is all rock, above us and on the sides. At one spot, the pickaxe marks change direction. That's where the two groups met!

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the Siloam inscription.

doc.body: It tells how two teams with pickaxes dug inside the rock and met.

evidence.title: Tunnel sketch
evidence.description: The tunnel runs from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam.

cases.wrongAccusation: Read Elena's notebook again: how many groups were there, what did they use, and where were they?

reward.title: Hezekiah's Tunnel
reward.copy: In 1880, a boy exploring a tunnel in Jerusalem found an inscription on the wall. It tells how two groups dug through the rock from both ends until they met, to bring water from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam. The tunnel is more than five hundred meters long. Many experts think it is the work of King Hezekiah: 2 Kings 20:20 and 2 Chronicles 32:30 tell how he brought water into the city through a channel. Years later, the stone was cut out of the wall. Today it is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

cases.title: The Broken Stone of Moab
cases.summary: A black stone full of letters breaks into pieces, but its words are saved.
cases.brief: In 1868, a black stone with many letters turned up in Dibon. Soon after, someone broke it into pieces. Even so, its words were not lost. Now we need to know what saved them.
cases.objective: What saved the words of the stone when it was broken?

evidence.title: The land of Dibon
evidence.description: Dry hills east of the Dead Sea, where the Moabites lived.

evidence.title: The traveler
evidence.description: A European missionary traveled the region on horseback with a guide.

evidence.title: Piece of black stone
evidence.description: Piece of hard black stone, with rows of carved letters. Its edges are broken.

evidence.title: Clay tablet
evidence.description: Pale clay tablet with rows of wedge-shaped marks. It fits in one hand.

evidence.title: Parchment scroll
evidence.description: Whole cream-colored parchment scroll, handwritten with dark ink.

evidence.title: Sheets of grey paper
evidence.description: Thick grey paper, torn into several pieces that were put back together like a puzzle. With light from the side you can see rows of letters.

evidence.title: The stone put back together
evidence.description: The stone rebuilt, with lighter parts where pieces were missing.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: How to copy carved letters without writing.

doc.body: The scholar Charles Clermont-Ganneau sent a helper to copy the stone. He pressed wet paper against the letters. When it dries, the paper keeps their shape, with no ink. This is called a squeeze.

evidence.title: Message from Tomás
evidence.description: Tomás saw the squeeze in a museum.

doc.body: Professor: I saw the squeeze! It is grey paper, torn into several pieces, because it was pulled off the stone while still wet. It has no ink, but the letters stand out in relief.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the squeeze of the stone.

doc.body: It was made before the stone was broken. It helped to read the lost parts.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: The stone breaks into pieces.

doc.headline: Ancient stone broken in Moab
doc.body: It was heated and then soaked with cold water until it cracked. Several pieces have already been gathered. Luckily, a copy of its letters had been made before.

cases.wrongAccusation: Look again at Elena's notebook: what material was the copy made of, and what did its letters look like?

reward.title: The Mesha Stone
reward.copy: In 1868, the missionary Frederick Klein saw a black stone with 34 lines of letters in Dibon, in today's Jordan. Mesha, king of Moab, had it carved about 2,800 years ago. It says that Omri, king of Israel, had ruled over Moab, and that Mesha broke free. Before the stone was broken, a paper squeeze was made, and with it and the pieces that were gathered, the stone was put back together. In 2 Kings 3 the Bible also speaks of Mesha, king of Moab, who raised sheep and stopped paying tribute to Israel. Today it is in the Louvre Museum, in Paris.

cases.title: The House of David
cases.summary: A stone with letters turns up hidden among the other stones of Tel Dan.
cases.brief: In 1993, in the ruins of Tel Dan, a woman on the team saw letters on a dark stone. That stone names the "house of David". Now we need to know where in the ancient city it turned up.
cases.objective: Where in Tel Dan did the stone turn up?

evidence.title: Tel Dan
evidence.description: A green hill with ancient ruins, in northern Israel.

evidence.title: The surveyor
evidence.description: Gila Cook measured the ruins to draw the team's plans.

evidence.title: The stream
evidence.description: Fresh, clear water running over smooth stones, under tall trees and ferns.

evidence.title: The city entrance
evidence.description: Two dark stone towers with a passage between them. In front there is a small paved square.

evidence.title: The great platform
evidence.description: Tall square platform of well-cut stones, with a wide stairway on one side.

evidence.title: The stone with letters
evidence.description: Piece of dark basalt with carved letters. Its edges are broken. It is about 32 centimeters tall.

evidence.title: The dig
evidence.description: Avraham Biran's team worked at Tel Dan for many summers.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: How the stone turned up.

doc.body: Gila Cook, from Avraham Biran's team, saw letters on a dark stone. It was set in a low wall, next to the city gate. Someone had used it as just another stone!

evidence.title: Message from Lía
evidence.description: Lía toured the ruins with the guide.

doc.body: Professor: the guide told us the stone was broken and was used to build a wall. We saw it: it is right next to the city entrance, facing a little plaza.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the Tel Dan stele.

doc.body: Written in Aramaic. It names a king of Israel and the house of David.

evidence.title: Plan of Tel Dan
evidence.description: Where each part of the ancient city is.

cases.wrongAccusation: Read Elena's notebook again and look at the plan: which part of the city was the wall next to?

reward.title: The Tel Dan Stele
reward.copy: In July 1993, at Tel Dan in northern Israel, Gila Cook, from archaeologist Avraham Biran's team, saw letters on a basalt stone set in a wall next to the city gate. It was part of a stele written in Aramaic about 2,800 years ago. The next year, two more pieces turned up. The stone speaks of a king of Israel and of the "house of David". It was a great find: David's name outside the Bible. In 2 Samuel 7, God promises David that his house, his family of kings, will last. Today it is in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

cases.title: The Boat in the Mud
cases.summary: A very old wooden boat turns up on the shore of the Sea of Galilee.
cases.brief: In 1986 there was very little rain and the water of the Sea of Galilee went down. Two fisherman brothers saw an ancient boat in the mud. Its wood was so soft that it could break. Now we need to know how they took it to the museum.
cases.objective: How did they take the boat to the museum without breaking it?

evidence.title: The dry shore
evidence.description: The lake's water went down and uncovered a lot of mud.

evidence.title: The fisherman brothers
evidence.description: Moshe and Yuval Lufan were walking along the shore and saw something in the mud.

evidence.title: The boat in the mud
evidence.description: It is about 8 meters long. Its wooden planks have many patches.

evidence.title: Photo A
evidence.description: A crane lifts the dark wooden boat with ropes, toward a truck on the shore.

evidence.title: Photo B
evidence.description: A long white bundle, shaped like a boat, floats on the lake. A motorboat pulls it slowly.

evidence.title: Photo C
evidence.description: The dark wooden boat floats low in the calm water. You can see its planks and ribs.

evidence.title: Photo D
evidence.description: Several people carry dark wooden planks on their shoulders along the muddy shore.

evidence.title: The museum
evidence.description: Today the boat rests in a hall of the Ginosar museum.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: The problem with wet wood.

doc.body: The wood spent centuries under water. It is as soft as wet bread: if they lift it like this, it breaks. That's why they covered it all in white foam, like a cocoon.

evidence.title: Message from Tomás
evidence.description: Tomás saw photos of the move.

doc.body: Professor: they didn't put it on any truck! The boat, wrapped in foam, went floating across the lake, like a giant toy boat.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the Galilee Boat.

doc.body: Made mostly of cedar and oak, with many patches. It is from the time of Jesus.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: The boat's journey.

doc.headline: Ancient boat travels across the lake
doc.body: Covered in white foam, the boat floated across the water to Ginosar. There it was placed in a pool so its wood would not dry out too fast.

cases.wrongAccusation: Read Elena's notebook and the news again: what did they cover it with, and how did it travel?

reward.title: The Galilee Boat
reward.copy: In January 1986 there was very little rain and the Sea of Galilee dropped a lot. The brothers Moshe and Yuval Lufan, fishermen from Ginosar, saw the shape of a wooden boat in the mud. It is about eight meters long and comes from the time of Jesus. No one knows who used it, but it shows what fishing boats were like back then. Mark 4 tells how Jesus and his disciples were crossing the lake in a boat when a great storm came, and he calmed the wind and the waves. Today the boat is at the Yigal Allon Museum, in Ginosar.

cases.title: The pool under the pipe
cases.summary: Workers fix a pipe and the digger hits ancient stone.
cases.brief: In 2004, in Jerusalem, some workers were digging to fix a water pipe. Something very old appeared under the ground. The team has pictures of four places with water in the area: only one is the Pool of Siloam from the time of Jesus.
cases.objective: Which of these places is the Pool of Siloam from the time of Jesus?

evidence.title: The city hillside
evidence.description: Southern part of the City of David, the oldest area of Jerusalem.

evidence.title: The digger stops
evidence.description: Year 2004: a small digger opens a trench for a water pipe.

evidence.title: The water tunnel
evidence.description: Narrow tunnel cut into the rock, with clear water running along the floor. It was dug about 700 years before Jesus.

evidence.title: The small pool
evidence.description: Small pool of greenish water, between tall stone walls, with pieces of broken columns.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What kind of place the Pool of Siloam was.

doc.body: John 9 tells how Jesus sent a blind man to wash in the Pool of Siloam. A pool is still water open to the sky, where people can go in. The water did not start there: it came through Hezekiah's tunnel.

evidence.title: Coins in the plaster
evidence.description: Three worn bronze coins, with bits of white plaster. They came from the 2004 dig.

evidence.title: Steps under the ground
evidence.description: A large open place. Many long stone steps go down, one after another, to a little water.

evidence.title: Tomás's letter
evidence.description: Tomás walked around the area with a guide.

doc.body: Professor: the guide showed us a small pool, between walls, with broken columns. It was made about 400 years after Jesus! Then we went down to what Eli Shukron and Ronny Reich found in 2004. That is much older.

evidence.title: The round well
evidence.description: Round, deep well with a low stone rim. A rope and a wooden bucket hang above it.

evidence.title: Pool record
evidence.description: Facts about the 2004 find.

fields: Already there in the time of Jesus
doc.body: The coins are from about a hundred years before Jesus. Very close by there is another pool, small and with columns, that was made centuries later: it is not the one in the Gospel.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: A newspaper tells about the find.

doc.headline: Pool where a blind man came back seeing is found
doc.body: Under the ground of Jerusalem an ancient pool appeared, open to the sky, right where Hezekiah's tunnel ends. According to the Gospel of John, Jesus sent a blind man to wash in the Pool of Siloam.

cases.wrongAccusation: You need two facts. Elena's notebook says what kind of place it was. Tomás's letter and the record say when each one was made. Look for the place that fits both.

reward.title: The Pool of Siloam
reward.copy: In 2004, workers fixing a pipe in Jerusalem found stone steps. The archaeologists Eli Shukron and Ronny Reich saw that they belonged to the Pool of Siloam from the time of Jesus. The coins in the plaster helped to tell how old it was. John 9 tells how Jesus put mud on the eyes of a man who had been born blind and sent him to wash in the Pool of Siloam; the man came back able to see. Today you can see the steps in the City of David. Much of the pool is still under the ground.

cases.title: The porches of Bethesda
cases.summary: A famous pool from the Gospel, and four models that do not look alike.
cases.brief: The Gospel of John tells about a pool in Jerusalem called Bethesda, surrounded by porches. For a long time nobody knew what it looked like. Its remains appeared next to the Church of Saint Anne, and now the team has four models.
cases.objective: Which model shows what the Pool of Bethesda was like?
meta: Next to the Church of Saint Anne, Jerusalem

evidence.title: The ruins by Saint Anne
evidence.description: Very deep stone remains, next to a pale stone church in Jerusalem.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What a porch is and where they were.

doc.body: A porch is a walkway with a roof, held up by a row of columns. Experts draw Bethesda with porches on the four outer sides, so people could walk in the shade.

evidence.title: Model A
evidence.description: Model A: a round pool of blue water, with a stone rim.

evidence.title: The wall in the middle
evidence.description: Among the ruins you can see a thick rock wall that separates two pools.

evidence.title: Model B
evidence.description: Model B: a square pool. Along each of its sides runs a walkway with white columns.

evidence.title: Model C
evidence.description: Model C: two rectangular pools, side by side. It has white columns all around and another row on top of the middle wall.

evidence.title: Model D
evidence.description: Model D: two rectangular pools, side by side, with a wall in the middle. One row of white columns runs along one of its sides.

evidence.title: Lía's letter
evidence.description: Lía went down to see the ruins.

doc.body: Professor: today I went down with Tomás to see the ruins. It is not just one pool! There are two, side by side. In the middle there is a rock wall so thick you can walk on top of it.

evidence.title: Pool record
evidence.description: What we know about the pool.

fields: Next to the Church of Saint Anne
doc.body: John 5 tells that many sick people gathered there, under the porches. Jesus healed one of them.

evidence.title: Sketch of the pools
evidence.description: Tomás's drawing seen from above.

evidence.title: The city gate
evidence.description: A gate in the wall of the old city, a few steps from the ruins.

cases.wrongAccusation: You missed one fact. Lía's letter says how many pools there were. Elena's notebook says on which sides the porches were. Look for the model that fits both.

reward.title: The Pool of Bethesda
reward.copy: John 5 tells that in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate, there was a pool called Bethesda with five porches. There Jesus healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years: he told him to get up, pick up his mat and walk. For centuries nobody knew well what it looked like. Since the late 1800s, next to the Church of Saint Anne, archaeologists have uncovered two large pools separated by a wall. Today you can visit its ruins in the old city of Jerusalem.

cases.title: The theater stone
cases.summary: A stone used as a step held a famous name.
cases.brief: In 1961, an Italian team was digging in the Roman theater of Caesarea, by the sea. On a stairway of the theater there was a very special stone. The team has pictures of four ancient objects: only one is that stone.
cases.objective: Which is the stone that names Pontius Pilate?

evidence.title: The theater by the sea
evidence.description: Roman theater of Caesarea, with stone seats facing the sea.

evidence.title: Rounded black stone
evidence.description: Tall slab of black stone, with a rounded top. It has rows of ancient carved letters.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What stone it is made of.

doc.body: The Pilate stone is limestone, a pale, cream-colored stone, like sand. There was plenty of it in Caesarea. Centuries later, someone used it as just another step of the theater.

evidence.title: The theater steps
evidence.description: Here, in 1961, a stone used as a step was found.

evidence.title: Piece of a column
evidence.description: Piece of a white stone column, round like a drum. It is lying on the sand.

evidence.title: Telegram from 1961
evidence.description: Message sent from Caesarea.

doc.body: ITALIAN TEAM OF ANTONIO FROVA FINDS ON THEATER STAIRWAY STONE WITH LATIN LETTERS, THE SAME AS OUR ALPHABET. IT NAMES PONTIUS PILATE.

evidence.title: Rectangular block
evidence.description: Rectangular cream-colored stone block, about 80 centimeters tall, with rows of worn letters. Its left side is broken.

evidence.title: Clay tablet
evidence.description: Small tablet of brown clay, with wedge-shaped marks. It fits in one hand.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the stone.

doc.body: It names Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea, and a building in honor of the emperor Tiberius. Part of the text was lost with the broken piece.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: A newspaper tells about the find.

doc.headline: A theater stone names Pilate
doc.body: Italian archaeologists found in Caesarea a stone with Latin letters carved in rows. It is from his own time and has the name of the governor who judged Jesus.

evidence.title: The aqueduct
evidence.description: Roman water channel on arches, on the beach of Caesarea.

cases.wrongAccusation: Cross two papers: Elena's notebook says what stone it is, and the telegram says what is carved on it. Only one piece fits both.

reward.title: The Pilate Stone
reward.copy: In 1961, the Italian team of Antonio Frova was digging in the Roman theater of Caesarea. On a stairway they found a block of pale stone that had been used as a step. Its Latin letters name Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea, and a building in honor of the emperor Tiberius. Matthew 27 tells how Jesus was brought before the governor Pilate, who questioned him and judged him. The original stone is in the Israel Museum, in Jerusalem. There is a copy in Caesarea.

cases.title: The box with the flowers
cases.summary: A park, a hidden cave and several stone boxes.
cases.brief: In 1990, some workers were making a road in a park south of Jerusalem. The ground sank and an ancient cave appeared with several stone boxes. One of them has a name that appears in the Gospels. The team compares four boxes from the museum.
cases.objective: Which is the box of Joseph, son of Caiaphas?

evidence.title: The pine park
evidence.description: Park with pine trees south of Jerusalem. The ground caved in here.

evidence.title: The cave entrance
evidence.description: A cave cut into the rock, with a small opening to go in.

evidence.title: Plain box
evidence.description: Pale stone box, with a flat lid and smooth sides. It came from the 1990 cave.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What an ossuary is and how Caiaphas's one is decorated.

doc.body: An ossuary is a stone box where families kept the bones of their dead. The box of Joseph, son of Caiaphas, is decorated with rosettes: flowers carved inside a circle, like a wheel.

evidence.title: One-circle box
evidence.description: Stone box with one circle of flowers carved on the front. It was found in 1953, on the Mount of Olives.

evidence.title: Two-circle box
evidence.description: Limestone box with two big circles of flowers and a carved border around them. It came from the 1990 cave.

evidence.title: Zigzag box
evidence.description: Stone box with bands of zigzag lines carved on the front. It came from the 1990 cave.

evidence.title: Tomás's letter
evidence.description: Tomás saw the box at the museum.

doc.body: Professor: at the museum we saw Caiaphas's box. It has flowers carved inside circles, like wheels! On one side there are scratched letters, as if made with a nail. They say "Joseph, son of Caiaphas".

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the box.

doc.body: The letters, in Aramaic, say "Joseph, son of Caiaphas". The historian Josephus called the high priest Joseph Caiaphas.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: A newspaper tells about the find.

doc.headline: Ancient cave kept the name of Caiaphas
doc.body: Workers making a road in the Peace Forest discovered a cave with stone boxes. One of those boxes has scratched letters with the name of Caiaphas.

evidence.title: The museum hall
evidence.description: Hall of the Israel Museum where the box is shown today.

cases.wrongAccusation: You missed crossing two facts: how the box is decorated (Elena's notebook) and where it came from (the museum record). Look at the description of each box.

reward.title: The Caiaphas Ossuary
reward.copy: In 1990, in the Peace Forest, south of Jerusalem, an ancient cave with several ossuaries was opened by accident. The archaeologist Zvi Greenhut studied it. On the most decorated box someone had scratched «Joseph, son of Caiaphas». Many experts think it belonged to the family of the high priest Caiaphas. John 18 tells how Jesus was brought before Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. Today the box is in the Israel Museum, in Jerusalem.

cases.title: The king who let them go home
cases.summary: A king of Persia wrote down that peoples could go back home.
cases.brief: In 1879, Hormuzd Rassam was digging in the ruins of Babylon, in what is now Iraq. Out of the earth came a clay object that today is called the Cyrus Cylinder. The team has pictures of four ancient clay objects.
cases.objective: Which of these clay objects is the Cyrus Cylinder?

evidence.title: The ruins of Babylon
evidence.description: Mounds of earth and bricks by the Euphrates River.

evidence.title: The 1879 dig
evidence.description: Workers with baskets and shovels take earth out of the ruins. A round clay piece came out of the earth.

evidence.title: Flat tablet
evidence.description: Flat, rectangular clay tablet with wedge marks. It fits in the palm of your hand.

evidence.title: Elena's notebook
evidence.description: What shape the Cyrus Cylinder has.

doc.body: The Cyrus Cylinder is round: it has no corners and no flat sides. If you push it on the table, it rolls. It has cracks because it was found broken.

evidence.title: Standing prism
evidence.description: Standing clay prism with six flat sides, like a giant pencil. It is covered with wedge marks.

evidence.title: Jar with handles
evidence.description: Round clay jar with two small handles. It is about 30 centimeters tall.

evidence.title: Piece lying down
evidence.description: Long clay piece lying on its side, covered with tiny marks. It has cracks and a few small bits are missing. It is about 23 centimeters long.

evidence.title: Lía's letter
evidence.description: Lía went to the museum in London.

doc.body: Professor: I am at the British Museum, in London. I saw the Cyrus Cylinder! All over, it is full of tiny wedges, in tight rows. There is not a single empty space.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the cylinder.

doc.body: Cyrus, king of Persia, tells that he took Babylon and let peoples who had been taken far away return to their land.

evidence.title: The way back
evidence.description: Lía's simple map.

doc.header: Lía's map · from Babylon to Jerusalem
marks: Babylon: the cylinder was found here
Jerusalem: where the Jews went back

evidence.title: The London museum
evidence.description: Hall of the British Museum where the cylinder is today.

cases.wrongAccusation: You missed crossing two facts: the shape (Elena's notebook) and what is on it (Lía's letter or the record). One piece has the shape but not the other thing; another one is the other way around.

reward.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
reward.copy: In 1879, Hormuzd Rassam found in Babylon a clay cylinder written by order of Cyrus, king of Persia, after he took the city in 539 BC. The text tells that Cyrus let peoples who had been carried far away go back to their lands. It does not name the Jews, but it shows the same way of acting that Ezra 1 describes: Cyrus allowed the Jews to go back to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple. Today the cylinder is in the British Museum, in London.

cases.title: The King Who Shut Hezekiah In
cases.summary: A king of Assyria wrote his own version of the story of King Hezekiah.
cases.brief: In a museum, three clay objects from Assyria lost their labels. One of them is the prism of King Sennacherib, which talks about Hezekiah, king of Judah. Read the clues and find it.
cases.objective: Which of the three clay objects is Sennacherib's?

evidence.title: The hills of Nineveh
evidence.description: Earth mounds by the Tigris River. Underneath were the palaces of the kings of Assyria.

evidence.title: The museum room
evidence.description: Three display cases with no labels. Each one holds a clay object with wedge-shaped writing.

evidence.title: Object A: the barrel
evidence.description: Baked clay, round like a barrel lying on its side. It is 38 cm long. It is covered in little wedge-shaped marks.

evidence.title: Object B: the tablet
evidence.description: Brown baked clay, with a front side and a back side. It is 9 cm: it fits in the palm of your hand.

evidence.title: Object C: the column
evidence.description: Reddish baked clay, standing upright like a column. It is 38 cm tall. The wedges run in very tight rows.

evidence.title: An Assyrian scribe
evidence.description: Scribes marked soft clay with a pointed reed. Then they baked it so it would last.

evidence.title: The camp of 1830
evidence.description: European travelers camped next to the ruins to look for ancient objects.

evidence.title: The professor's notebook
evidence.description: How the king's text was written.

doc.body: Sennacherib's text runs in straight rows on flat faces, one next to the other. To read it all, you have to turn the piece around. A round surface does not work for that.
doc.footer: Look closely at the shape of each object.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: The label that fell off a display case.

doc.body: It tells about the wars of the king of Assyria. It mentions Hezekiah, king of Judah.

evidence.title: Tomás's letter
evidence.description: Tomás measured the objects.

doc.body: Professor: I measured the three objects. How strange! The barrel lying down and the standing column are the same size: 38 cm. The tablet is only 9 cm and fits in my hand.

evidence.title: Old news
evidence.description: What the text on the prism says.

doc.headline: A king of Assyria talks about Hezekiah
doc.body: The text says Sennacherib took many cities of Judah and shut King Hezekiah up in Jerusalem. But it does not say he took Jerusalem.

cases.wrongAccusation: That object matches one thing, but not the other. Check the size on the museum record and read in the notebook what kind of surface the text was written on.

reward.title: Sennacherib's Prism
reward.copy: Sennacherib, king of Assyria, had his wars written on clay prisms. In 1830, the British colonel Robert Taylor obtained one in the ruins of Nineveh, near today's Mosul, in Iraq. The text says that in 701 BC the king took 46 cities of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage." But it does not say he entered Jerusalem. 2 Kings 18 and 19 tell how Hezekiah prayed to God and Sennacherib went back to his land without taking the city. Today this prism is in the British Museum in London.

cases.title: The Black Stone of Nimrud
cases.summary: A king of Israel appears on a black stone from Assyria.
cases.brief: The black obelisk of King Shalmaneser III has many carved pictures. One of them shows Jehu, king of Israel, or a messenger sent by him. Tomás and Lía took photos of four pictures, but they mixed them up.
cases.objective: Which of the four carved pictures shows Jehu, king of Israel?

evidence.title: The hill of Nimrud
evidence.description: A big mound by the Tigris River. Kalhu, a city of the kings of Assyria, stood there.

evidence.title: The whole obelisk
evidence.description: A black stone almost two meters tall, with four sides and a stepped top. It has five rows of carved panels.

evidence.title: Picture 1: the camels
evidence.description: Men walk upright in a line, bringing two-humped camels. Lía took this photo in the top row.

evidence.title: Picture 2: the lion
evidence.description: A lion leaps on a deer among trees. Lía took this photo in the fourth row.

evidence.title: Picture 3: the kneeling man
evidence.description: A king holds a bowl; behind him, a servant shades him with a parasol. Lía took this photo in the second row.

evidence.title: Picture 4: the elephant
evidence.description: An elephant and some monkeys walk in a line. Lía took this photo in the third row.

evidence.title: A digger in 1846
evidence.description: Workers dug long trenches to find the buried palaces.

evidence.title: The professor's notebook
evidence.description: What the panels on the obelisk show.

doc.body: Each row of panels shows a different people bringing gifts to King Shalmaneser. In the row of Jehu, the gifts are brought by people, not only animals.
doc.footer: First, pick out the panels with people.

evidence.title: Lía's letter
evidence.description: Lía wrote down where she took each photo.

doc.body: Professor: I took the photos from top to bottom and wrote down the row of each one. But I mixed them up. Two panels have people in them; in the other two I only see animals.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the obelisk.

doc.body: The text that names Jehu is in the second row. In his panel, a man bows until his forehead touches the ground in front of the king.

evidence.title: News from 1846
evidence.description: Layard's discovery.

doc.headline: A black stone comes out of the ground at Nimrud
doc.body: The explorer Austen Henry Layard found a black obelisk full of carved pictures. Later, people learned that one of them mentions Jehu, king of Israel.

cases.wrongAccusation: That panel has some of what you are looking for, but not all. Check on the museum record which row Jehu is in, and compare with what Lía wrote on each photo.

reward.title: The Black Obelisk
reward.copy: In 1846, the explorer Austen Henry Layard found a black stone almost two meters tall at Nimrud, Iraq. It is the obelisk of King Shalmaneser III of Assyria. Its carved pictures show peoples bringing him gifts. In one, a man bows to the ground, and the text names Jehu. It may be Jehu himself or a messenger sent by him. It is one of the oldest known pictures of an Israelite. Jehu's story is told in 2 Kings 9 and 10. Today the obelisk is in the British Museum in London.

cases.title: Messages at the Gate
cases.summary: Soldiers of Judah wrote messages to each other while the army of Babylon was coming.
cases.brief: At the gate of the city of Lachish, letters from about 2,600 years ago were found. But they were not written on paper. Lía put three ancient objects on the table, and only one is like the Lachish letters.
cases.objective: Which of the three objects is like the Lachish letters?

evidence.title: The hill of Lachish
evidence.description: A tall hill among green fields. On top stood a walled city of Judah.

evidence.title: The city gate
evidence.description: Remains of the great gate with its guard rooms. The black layer is ash from a big fire. The letters came out of that ash.

evidence.title: Object A: clay tablet
evidence.description: Baked clay, flat and hard. It has sunken wedge-shaped marks, made by pressing into soft clay.

evidence.title: Object B: piece of a jar
evidence.description: A hard, curved piece of a reddish clay jar, with uneven edges. It has some lines of dark letters, written by hand.

evidence.title: Object C: papyrus roll
evidence.description: A pale yellow rolled sheet made from a plant. It has lines of letters written in ink.

evidence.title: A soldier of Judah
evidence.description: Soldiers at the lookout posts sent messages to Lachish.

evidence.title: Fires on the hills
evidence.description: Cities sent warnings to each other with fires lit on high places.

evidence.title: The professor's notebook
evidence.description: How the soldiers wrote.

doc.body: The soldiers wrote with a reed dipped in black ink. They used the letters of ancient Hebrew, like those of the Bible. They did not press marks into clay.
doc.footer: Next, see what could come out of a fire in one piece.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about letter number 4.

doc.body: The soldier says he is watching for the fire signals of Lachish and can no longer see those of Azekah.

evidence.title: Lía's letter
evidence.description: Lía touched the three objects and asked something.

doc.body: Professor: the scroll is soft and bends. The tablet and the jar piece are hard. You told me the plant sheet burns like paper, but baked clay can stand fire: that is why it is baked in an oven.

evidence.title: Cities of Judah
evidence.description: Lachish, Azekah and Jerusalem.

marks: Gate of Lachish: the letters were here
Azekah: its fire could no longer be seen

cases.wrongAccusation: That object matches part of it. The letters came out of the ash of a fire. Check what the soldiers wrote with and, in Lía's letter, what can survive fire.

reward.title: The Lachish Letters
reward.copy: In 1935, James Leslie Starkey's expedition found several letters at the gate of Lachish, written in ink on pieces of jars. They are about 2,600 years old, from the time when the army of Babylon was attacking Judah. In one, a soldier says he is watching for the fire signals of Lachish and can no longer see those of Azekah. Jeremiah 34:7 tells that at that time only three walled cities were still standing: Jerusalem, Lachish and Azekah. Today the letters are kept in the British Museum in London and in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

cases.title: The Hidden Blessing
cases.summary: A very small object held the oldest Bible text we know.
cases.brief: In a cave in Jerusalem, people found jewelry, jars and other small objects. Among them was something that held a blessing from the Bible. Tomás left three objects on the table: only one is the one you are looking for.
cases.objective: Which of the three objects had the blessing written on it?

evidence.title: The slope of Ketef Hinnom
evidence.description: A rocky slope by the Hinnom Valley, next to the old city of Jerusalem.

evidence.title: Inside the cave
evidence.description: A cave cut into the rock, with stone benches. Under one bench there was a hollow full of objects.

evidence.title: Object A: the bracelet
evidence.description: An open metal ring, covered in a green layer. It is about 6 cm wide. It came out of the pit under the bench.

evidence.title: Object B: the little tube
evidence.description: A little gray metal tube, shiny with dark spots. It is a very thin sheet, rolled up. It is shorter than a little finger. It came out of the pit under the bench.

evidence.title: Object C: the lamp
evidence.description: A reddish clay oil lamp, with a folded edge for the wick. It is about 12 cm. It came out of the pit under the bench.

evidence.title: A young volunteer
evidence.description: In 1979, children and teenagers helped. One of them, 13 years old, found the hollow with the objects.

evidence.title: In the laboratory
evidence.description: Unrolling the little tubes without breaking them took about three years.

evidence.title: The professor's notebook
evidence.description: What the blessing was written on.

doc.body: The blessing was engraved with a fine point on metal, not on clay. Because the piece was rolled up very tightly, it had to be unrolled to read the letters.
doc.footer: Check the three objects from the pit.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about the little scrolls.

doc.body: Very fine letters are engraved on them. They say a blessing like the one in Numbers 6.

evidence.title: Tomás's letter
evidence.description: Tomás cleaned the objects with the professor.

doc.body: Professor: two objects are metal, but they are different colors. You explained that, over the years, bronze turns green and silver turns gray with dark spots. The lamp is clay.

evidence.title: The news
evidence.description: What the little scrolls said.

doc.headline: The oldest blessing is read
doc.body: At last, the writing on the little scrolls could be read. It asks the Lord to bless, keep and give peace. They are about 400 years older than the Dead Sea Scrolls.

cases.wrongAccusation: Not that one. First look at what each object is made of. Then check Tomás's letter for the color each metal turns over the years.

reward.title: The Silver Scrolls
reward.copy: In 1979, the archaeologist Gabriel Barkay was digging in some caves at Ketef Hinnom, next to Jerusalem. A 13-year-old volunteer found a hollow full of objects, and among them were two little silver scrolls. Opening them without breaking them took about three years. They have a blessing scratched on them very much like the one in Numbers 6:24-26, which asks the Lord to bless, keep and give peace to his people. They are about 2,600 years old: the oldest Bible text known today. Today they are in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

cases.title: The Name Hidden in Ur
cases.summary: Some clay cylinders named King Belshazzar from the book of Daniel.
cases.brief: In 1854, clay cylinders of King Nabonidus turned up in the ancient city of Ur. They name his son Belshazzar, the king of the feast in Daniel 5. But which building were they hidden in?
cases.objective: In which of the three buildings of Ur were the cylinders hidden?

evidence.title: The ruins of Ur
evidence.description: A dry plain in southern Iraq. Ur, a very old city, stood there.

evidence.title: Building A: the house with a courtyard
evidence.description: A one-story house of mud bricks. Its four walls surround a courtyard in the middle.

evidence.title: Building B: the stepped tower
evidence.description: A huge mud-brick building with stepped levels, four corners and long stairways in front.

evidence.title: Building C: the underground tomb
evidence.description: A deep pit dug into the ground, with a stone chamber at the bottom and a ramp to go down.

evidence.title: A cylinder of Nabonidus
evidence.description: Baked clay shaped like a small barrel, covered in wedge-shaped writing.

evidence.title: Digging in 1854
evidence.description: Workers take bricks out of a very high corner, standing on a wooden ladder.

evidence.title: Belshazzar's feast
evidence.description: In Daniel 5, King Belshazzar throws a great feast in Babylon.

evidence.title: The professor's notebook
evidence.description: How Nabonidus hid the cylinders.

doc.body: Nabonidus put the cylinders between the mud bricks, one in each of the four corners of the building he repaired. That way, whoever repaired it later would know who had done it before.
doc.footer: Look for brick walls with four corners.

evidence.title: Lía's letter
evidence.description: Lía walked through the three buildings.

doc.body: Professor: the courtyard house is made of brick and has four corners, like a square. The tomb is stone and underground. From the top of the tower you can see the whole plain.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Facts about one cylinder.

doc.body: Nabonidus says he repaired the tower of the Moon god's temple. He asks his god for a long life for himself and for his eldest son, Belshazzar.

evidence.title: Map of Ur
evidence.description: The buildings of Ur.

cases.wrongAccusation: That building matches part of it. Read on the museum record which building Nabonidus repaired, and find it on the map.

reward.title: The Cylinders of Nabonidus
reward.copy: In 1854, Taylor, a British official in Basra, dug into the ziggurat of Ur, in southern Iraq. In the corners of the tower he found clay cylinders of King Nabonidus of Babylon. In them, the king asks for a long life for himself and for his eldest son, Belshazzar. For a long time, Belshazzar's name was known only from the Bible. Daniel 5 tells about his great feast and the hand that wrote on the wall. Today one of these cylinders is in the British Museum in London.

cases.title: King Hezekiah's seal
cases.summary: A clay mark held the name of a king of Judah.
cases.brief: At a dig by the walls of Jerusalem, volunteers wash and sift the soil from an ancient garbage dump. Among pebbles and broken pottery, several pieces with pictures turned up. One of them carries the mark of King Hezekiah's seal.
cases.objective: Which of the pieces is the mark of King Hezekiah's seal?

evidence.title: The Ophel
evidence.description: Dig area at the foot of Jerusalem's southern walls.

evidence.title: Volunteer at the sieve
evidence.description: She washes the soil with water over a fine mesh so nothing small gets lost.

evidence.title: Piece with a lion
evidence.description: A little lump of dark clay, the size of a fingernail. A walking lion is stamped on it. On the back it has fine string marks.

evidence.title: Jar handle with a winged sun
evidence.description: A thick, curved handle of a reddish clay jar, as big as a hand. A sun with two wings is stamped on it, inside an oval.

evidence.title: Piece with a winged sun
evidence.description: An oval lump of dark clay, the size of a fingernail. A sun with two open wings is stamped on it. On the back it has fine string marks.

evidence.title: What stayed in the mesh
evidence.description: Pebbles, broken pottery and tiny bones from the ancient dump.

evidence.title: In the lab
evidence.description: An archaeologist looks at the small pieces through a big magnifier.

evidence.title: Lía's notebook
evidence.description: What Professor Elena told Lía about the drawing.

doc.body: Professor Elena says Hezekiah's seal had a sun with two wings. But careful: in his time, that winged sun was also stamped on other things of the king, like the handles of his jars.

evidence.title: Lab record
evidence.description: Facts about the piece with the king's name.

fields: Dump next to a royal building
doc.body: The letters say: "Belonging to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah." You read it with a magnifying glass.

evidence.title: The professor's letter
evidence.description: Elena explains how a document was closed.

doc.body: Dear Tomás and Lía: almost three thousand years ago, documents were rolled up and tied with a string. A lump of soft clay was put on top and the seal was pressed into it. When it dried, the lump came off loose, with the string marks on its back.

evidence.title: News from 2015
evidence.description: The announcement of the find.

doc.headline: Mark of King Hezekiah's seal found
doc.body: Archaeologist Eilat Mazar's team found the piece while sifting the soil of an ancient dump, near a royal building. It is the first mark of a seal of a king of Israel or Judah found in an excavation.

cases.wrongAccusation: That piece matches part of it. Check the drawing of the seal in Lía's notebook and, in the professor's letter, what the mark that closed a document was like.

reward.title: The mark of King Hezekiah's seal
reward.copy: In the Ophel area, by the southern walls of Jerusalem, archaeologist Eilat Mazar's team sifted the soil of an ancient dump. Out came a lump of clay about one centimeter wide, announced in 2015. It shows a sun with two wings and ancient Hebrew letters: "Belonging to Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, king of Judah". 2 Kings 18 tells how Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, trusted God like few other kings. It is the first seal mark of a king of Israel or Judah found in an archaeological dig. Today it is studied by archaeologists of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

cases.title: The name on the floor of Corinth
cases.summary: A man named Erastus paid for a stone floor and left his name written in it.
cases.brief: In the ancient city of Corinth, in Greece, there are many stones with letters. One of them carries the name of Erastus, a man who paid for the floor of a plaza. You have to find which one it is.
cases.objective: Which of the stones has the name of Erastus?

evidence.title: Ruins of Corinth
evidence.description: Ancient columns and, behind them, a tall rocky mountain.

evidence.title: The theater plaza
evidence.description: A plaza next to the ancient theater, with a floor of big stone slabs.

evidence.title: Column with letters
evidence.description: A piece of white marble column, standing upright. Around it there are letters carved into the stone.

evidence.title: Mosaic floor
evidence.description: A floor of small colored stones set together: they make red, black and cream flowers and vines. It was near the theater, under the dust.

evidence.title: Stamped tile
evidence.description: A broken red clay roof tile, the size of a hand. It has a rectangle with stamped letters.

evidence.title: Floor slab
evidence.description: A large flat slab of gray stone, set into the ground. It has a row of long grooves shaped like letters.

evidence.title: Site guide
evidence.description: She points at the floor of the plaza.

evidence.title: Tomás's notebook
evidence.description: What Tomás wrote down in the plaza.

doc.body: The guide says the stone of Erastus is part of a floor: people walked on top of it. Careful! Near the theater there is more than one ancient floor.

evidence.title: Inscription record
evidence.description: What the stone says and what it is made of.

doc.body: It says that Erastus, in return for his office of aedile, laid this pavement at his own expense. The bronze letters were set into grooves in the stone. Someone took the bronze and the grooves were left empty.

evidence.title: The professor's letter
evidence.description: Elena explains what an aedile was.

doc.body: Dear Tomás and Lía: an aedile took care of the streets, markets and buildings of the city. It was an important job. Erastus wanted to give thanks by paying for a pavement next to the theater. Look at how the letters are made.

evidence.title: Sketch of the area
evidence.description: Where Erastus's stone is.

marks: Erastus's slab, in the plaza floor

cases.wrongAccusation: That piece matches part of it, but not all. Check on the record what Erastus's letters looked like after someone took the bronze.

reward.title: The Erastus inscription
reward.copy: In 1929, archaeologists from the American School of Classical Studies at Athens found a limestone slab in Corinth, in a plaza next to the theater. It has a sentence in Latin: Erastus, in return for his post as aedile, laid this floor with his own money. The letters were bronze and were lost. In Romans 16:23, Paul, writing from Corinth, sends greetings from an Erastus who was the city treasurer. Many scholars think he could be the same man, though not all are sure. The slab is still in its place in Corinth today.

cases.title: The emperor's letter
cases.summary: A Roman emperor wrote a letter in stone that names Paul's judge.
cases.brief: At Delphi, in Greece, there was a great sanctuary with many written stones. A letter from Emperor Claudius mentions Gallio, the governor who heard Paul in Corinth. You have to find which stone holds that letter.
cases.objective: Which of the pieces holds the emperor's letter that names Gallio?

evidence.title: Delphi
evidence.description: Ruins of a sanctuary on a mountain slope.

evidence.title: Whole stone
evidence.description: A tall stone slab, with all four corners. It has rows of carved letters.

evidence.title: Bronze plaque
evidence.description: A greenish metal plaque. It has rows of engraved letters.

evidence.title: Stone pieces put together
evidence.description: Pieces of pale stone of different shapes, placed together on a panel. There are gaps between them. They have rows of carved letters.

evidence.title: Rebuilt vase
evidence.description: An orange clay vase, put together from glued pieces. It has dancers painted in black.

evidence.title: An old dig
evidence.description: Workers more than a hundred years ago lift stones at Delphi.

evidence.title: Museum conservator
evidence.description: She places each piece of stone next to the others, very carefully, to see if they fit.

evidence.title: Lía's notebook
evidence.description: What Lía learned at the museum.

doc.body: The emperor's letter was carved in stone, not in metal. It is in Greek, the language spoken in Delphi. The museum has several pieces with letters: you have to look at them carefully.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Details of Claudius's letter.

doc.body: Letter from Emperor Claudius to the city of Delphi. It names Gallio, his friend, as proconsul. Even though parts are missing, Gallio's name can be recognized.

evidence.title: The professor's letter
evidence.description: Elena explains why the stone matters.

doc.body: Dear Tomás and Lía: the letter of Claudius tells us what year Gallio was governing. That way we know roughly when Paul was in Corinth. Scholars took years to put together everything that was left of it.

cases.wrongAccusation: That piece matches part of it. Check on the museum record what state Claudius's letter was in, and in Lía's notebook what it is made of.

reward.title: The Gallio inscription
reward.copy: At Delphi, in Greece, French archaeologists found pieces of a stone with a letter from Emperor Claudius. It was first published in 1905. The letter is from AD 52 and names Gallio, his friend, as proconsul. Acts 18:12-17 tells how, when Gallio governed the region of Achaia, Paul was brought before him in Corinth, and Gallio refused to judge him. Thanks to this stone we can know, roughly, in which years Paul was in Corinth. Today the pieces are in the Delphi Archaeological Museum.

cases.title: The months of the fields
cases.summary: A written piece tells what was done in the fields each month of the year.
cases.brief: On the hill of Gezer, a tablet turned up that tells the farm work month by month: harvesting, sowing, pruning. But there are several written pieces on the camp table. You have to find which one is the tablet of the months.
cases.objective: Which of the pieces is the tablet of the farming months?

evidence.title: The hill of Gezer
evidence.description: An ancient hill surrounded by wheat fields and olive trees.

evidence.title: Big stone with letters
evidence.description: A slab of dark stone with a rounded top. It is almost as tall as a person. It has many rows of carved letters.

evidence.title: Clay tablet
evidence.description: A brown clay tablet. It fits in the palm of your hand. Its little marks are wedge-shaped.

evidence.title: Written pottery piece
evidence.description: A curved piece of a reddish clay jar, the size of a hand. It has lines of letters painted in black ink.

evidence.title: White stone tablet
evidence.description: A flat cream-colored stone tablet, the size of a hand. One corner is missing. It has lines of thin letters.

evidence.title: Barley harvest
evidence.description: This is how barley was harvested in spring, with sickles.

evidence.title: Olive harvest
evidence.description: In autumn, olives were gathered from the trees.

evidence.title: Tomás's notebook
evidence.description: What Tomás wrote about the tablet.

doc.body: The professor says the Gezer tablet is stone, but a soft stone: you can scratch it with a point. That is how its letters were made: scratched, not painted.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Details of the Gezer tablet.

fields: About 11 by 7 cm: it fits in a hand
doc.body: It is one of the oldest inscriptions found in Israel.

evidence.title: The professor's letter
evidence.description: Elena explains what the tablet says.

doc.body: Dear Tomás and Lía: the tablet names the jobs of the year. Two months of olive harvest, two of sowing, two of late sowing, one of cutting flax, one of barley harvest, one of the great harvest, two of pruning vines and one of summer fruit.

evidence.title: News from 1908
evidence.description: A newspaper reports the find.

doc.headline: The farmers' calendar comes out of the ground
doc.body: Irish archaeologist Robert Macalister, who is digging the hill of Gezer, found a written piece. It names the months of work in the fields.

cases.wrongAccusation: That piece matches part of it. Compare the size on the record with each piece, and read in Tomás's notebook what material it is and how the letters were made.

reward.title: The Gezer calendar
reward.copy: In 1908, archaeologist Robert Macalister was digging the hill of Gezer when he found a tablet of soft limestone, about 11 by 7 centimeters. It is about three thousand years old, and its scratched letters name the farm jobs: gathering olives, sowing, cutting flax, harvesting barley, pruning vines and picking summer fruit. It reminds us of Ecclesiastes 3, which says everything has its moment, including a time to plant. Today the tablet is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, in Turkey.

cases.title: King Jehoiachin's oil
cases.summary: In Babylon, someone wrote down how much oil was given to a king of Judah.
cases.brief: Jehoiachin, king of Judah, was taken as a prisoner to Babylon. In some storerooms near the city's great gate, food lists with his name turned up. You have to find which of the pieces is one of those lists.
cases.objective: Which of the pieces is the oil list for King Jehoiachin?

evidence.title: Ruins of Babylon
evidence.description: Brick walls by the Euphrates River.

evidence.title: The vaulted storerooms
evidence.description: Rooms with curved ceilings, near the city's great gate.

evidence.title: Brick with a lion
evidence.description: A large shiny blue brick with a yellow lion in relief. It was found near the great gate of the city.

evidence.title: Clay cylinder
evidence.description: A brown clay piece shaped like a barrel, about 20 cm long. It is covered in little wedge-shaped marks.

evidence.title: Flat tablet
evidence.description: Brown clay with slightly worn edges. It fits in the palm of your hand. It has rows of little wedge-shaped marks.

evidence.title: Ivory plaque
evidence.description: A flat cream-colored ivory plaque, the size of a palm. Palm leaves and lotus flowers are carved on it.

evidence.title: The scribe
evidence.description: A scribe presses a reed into soft clay. He holds the piece in the palm of his hand.

evidence.title: Sharing out the oil
evidence.description: Workers pour oil from big jars.

evidence.title: Lía's notebook
evidence.description: What Lía wrote down at the museum.

doc.body: The guide said the storeroom lists were written on soft clay, by pressing a reed into it: that makes little wedge-shaped marks. Then the clay dried.

evidence.title: Museum record
evidence.description: Details of the ration tablets.

doc.body: A list of oil for "Jehoiachin, king of the land of Judah" and for his five sons. It also names other people from Judah.

evidence.title: The professor's letter
evidence.description: Elena tells how the tablets were found.

doc.body: Dear Tomás and Lía: a German team led by Robert Koldewey dug in Babylon for many years. Hundreds of written pieces came out of the storerooms. Years later, Ernst Weidner read some of them and found the name of Jehoiachin. Careful: some very beautiful pieces were also found near that gate.

reward.title: King Jehoiachin's ration tablets
reward.copy: Between 1899 and 1917, a German team led by Robert Koldewey dug at Babylon. In some storerooms near the Ishtar Gate, many clay tablets came out. In 1939, Ernst Weidner showed that some were oil lists for "Jehoiachin, king of Judah", and for his five sons. The Bible tells that Jehoiachin was taken as a prisoner to Babylon, and 2 Kings 25:27-30 says that, years later, the king of Babylon released him from prison and gave him food every day for the rest of his life. Today the tablets are in the Museum of the Ancient Near East in Berlin.
